title: AI x Crypto
tagline: How AI models, agents and blockchains fit together, and how to judge the claims

modules.title: How large language models work
modules.summary: Large language models predict text one token at a time from patterns learned during training. Knowing this lets you judge what they can and cannot be trusted to do.
objectives: Explain what a token is and why models work with tokens rather than words
Describe next-token prediction as the core task of a language model
Tell the difference between training and inference
Explain why models hallucinate and why fluent output is not proof of accuracy
Use these ideas to question claims made about AI products

sections.heading: Tokens: the units a model reads
sections.body: A language model does not see letters or whole words the way you do. Text is first split into tokens, which are common chunks such as a short word, part of a longer word, or a punctuation mark. Each token is mapped to a number, and the model only ever works with these numbers. This is why models can struggle with tasks like counting letters in a word, since the letters may be hidden inside a single token. Prices and limits for AI services are usually measured in tokens, not words.

sections.heading: Predicting the next token
sections.body: At its core, a large language model does one job: given a sequence of tokens, it estimates how likely each possible next token is. It picks one, adds it to the sequence, and repeats the process until it stops. Long answers, code and summaries all come from this simple loop. A setting called temperature controls how adventurous the choice is, with low values favoring the most likely token and higher values adding variety. The model is not looking facts up in a database while it does this, it is producing text that fits the patterns it learned.

sections.heading: Training: learning the patterns
sections.body: Training is the expensive phase where the model learns. During pretraining, the model reads a very large body of text and repeatedly adjusts its internal numbers, called weights or parameters, to get better at predicting the next token. Later stages, such as fine-tuning on curated examples and learning from human feedback, shape the model into a helpful assistant. Training requires huge amounts of computing power and data, and it happens before the model is released. Once training ends, the model's knowledge is fixed at a point in time, often called its knowledge cutoff.

sections.heading: Inference: using the model
sections.body: Inference is what happens each time someone sends the model a prompt and it generates a reply. The weights do not change during inference, so a conversation does not retrain the model. Everything the model can consider for a reply has to fit in its context window, which is the maximum number of tokens it can process at once. Applications often add extra text to the context, such as instructions, documents or search results, before the user's message. Inference is much cheaper per request than training, but it adds up across millions of requests.

sections.heading: Why models hallucinate
sections.body: A hallucination is output that sounds confident and fluent but is false or made up, such as a fake citation or a wrong contract address. It happens because the model is optimized to produce plausible text, and a plausible-sounding answer is not always a correct one. The model has no built-in sense of whether it actually knows something. Hallucinations are more likely for rare facts, precise numbers, and events after the knowledge cutoff. In crypto, where a single wrong address or number can lose funds, any model output that matters should be checked against a reliable source.

sections.heading: Reasoning about AI claims
sections.body: These basics give you a toolkit for judging marketing claims. If a product says its AI knows today's prices, ask where that live data comes from, since the model itself has a cutoff. If a project says its model was trained on-chain, ask what was actually trained, where, and with what compute, because training large models is very resource-intensive. If a product says its AI cannot make mistakes, you already know that fluent output can still be wrong. Clear questions about tokens, training, inference and data sources cut through a lot of vague language.

concepts.definition: A chunk of text, such as a word piece or punctuation mark, that a language model reads and writes as a number.
The core task of a language model: estimating the most likely next token given the tokens so far.
The resource-heavy phase in which a model adjusts its weights by learning from large amounts of data.
Running an already trained model to produce output from a prompt, without changing its weights.
The maximum number of tokens a model can take into account at one time when generating a reply.
Fluent, confident model output that is false or invented.

example.title: Asking a chatbot for a token contract address
example.body: A user asks a general-purpose chatbot for the official contract address of a token. The model returns a correctly formatted address with total confidence, but it is not the real one, because the model generated a plausible string rather than looking it up. Scam tokens often copy names, so sending funds to an unverified address can be costly. The safe habit is to treat the answer as a starting point and confirm the address on the project's official site and a block explorer.

modules.title: AI agents that hold wallets
modules.summary: An AI agent is a model connected to tools that let it act, and a wallet is one of those tools. The key design question is how much the agent is allowed to do on its own.
objectives: Explain the difference between a chatbot and an agent
Describe how an agent framework turns model output into actions
Compare ways an agent can control a wallet, from raw keys to smart accounts
Explain session keys, spending limits and allowlists as permission tools
Describe how account abstraction helps keep agents within bounds

sections.heading: From chatbot to agent
sections.body: A chatbot answers questions, while an agent can take actions. An agent is a language model placed inside a loop: it reads a goal, decides on a step, calls a tool, reads the result, and decides what to do next. Tools can be anything a program can do, such as searching the web, reading a price feed, or signing a blockchain transaction. The model itself only produces text, and software around it turns that text into real actions. That surrounding software is where the safety rules must live.

sections.heading: Agent frameworks
sections.body: An agent framework is a software toolkit that handles the plumbing: connecting a model to tools, managing memory, and running the decide-act-observe loop. For crypto, frameworks add wallet tools such as checking a balance, sending tokens, or calling a smart contract. Coinbase's AgentKit is one example of a toolkit built to give agents wallets and onchain actions. The model typically outputs a structured tool call, the framework validates and executes it, and the result is fed back to the model. A framework is only as safe as the permissions it gives the agent.

sections.heading: Ways an agent can control funds
sections.body: The simplest and riskiest setup gives the agent a normal wallet whose private key sits on the same server as the agent. Anyone who compromises that server, or tricks the agent, can move everything in the wallet. A safer option uses a wallet service that holds the key and enforces policies, such as a maximum transfer size, before it will sign. Another option uses a smart contract wallet, where rules written into the contract decide which transactions are valid. In every case, the goal is to make sure a mistaken or manipulated model cannot exceed limits that a human set in advance.

sections.heading: Permissions and spending limits
sections.body: Good agent wallets follow the principle of least privilege: give the agent only the power it needs for its task. A spending limit caps how much value the agent can move per transaction or per day. An allowlist restricts which contracts or addresses it can interact with, so it cannot send funds to an unknown address even if instructed to. Time limits make permissions expire, so a forgotten agent does not keep its power forever. Large or unusual actions can require a human to approve them before they go through.

sections.heading: Account abstraction for agents
sections.body: Account abstraction lets a smart contract act as a user's account, with its own rules for which transactions are valid. On Ethereum, the ERC-4337 standard does this using a separate flow of user operations that bundlers submit through a shared entry point contract. A smart account can issue a session key: a separate key that is only valid for certain contracts, amounts and time windows. The agent holds the session key, while the owner's main key stays offline. Because the limits are checked on-chain by the account contract, they hold even if the agent's software is fully compromised.

sections.heading: Agents paying for services
sections.body: Agents also need to pay for things like data, APIs and compute without a human entering card details each time. Stablecoins suit this because they settle programmatically and in small amounts. The x402 protocol, introduced by Coinbase, uses the web's HTTP 402 Payment Required status code so a server can request payment and an agent can pay onchain and retry the request. Payment flows like this make spending limits even more important. An agent that can pay automatically can also overspend automatically if it is not bounded.

concepts.definition: A language model running in a loop with tools, so it can take actions toward a goal rather than only answer.
Software that connects a model to tools and memory and runs its decide-act-observe loop.
The practice of giving a system only the permissions it needs for its task and nothing more.
A secondary key with limited, often time-bound permissions that a smart account accepts on the owner's behalf.
Letting a smart contract serve as a user's account so it can define its own rules for valid transactions.
A list of approved contracts or addresses that an account is permitted to interact with.

example.title: A bounded agent wallet
example.body: A developer builds an agent that buys small amounts of data from paid APIs. Instead of giving it the main wallet, she sets up a smart account and issues a session key that can only spend a stablecoin, only up to a small daily cap, and only to three approved service addresses. One day the agent reads a malicious web page telling it to send all funds elsewhere. The agent tries, but the account contract rejects the transaction because the destination is not on the allowlist.

modules.title: Decentralized compute and GPU marketplaces
modules.summary: Decentralized compute networks match people who need processing power with people who have spare hardware. Their value depends on how they price work, pay providers and check that work was done.
objectives: Explain why GPUs matter for AI workloads
Describe the reverse auction model used by Akash
Describe the burn-and-mint payment model used by Render
Identify which AI workloads suit a distributed marketplace and which do not
Name the trust problems that marketplaces must solve

sections.heading: Why compute is the bottleneck
sections.body: Modern AI runs mostly on GPUs, chips that perform many simple calculations in parallel. Both training and inference consume large amounts of GPU time, and high-end GPUs are expensive and often in short supply. Traditional cloud providers rent this hardware, but pricing and access are set by a few large companies. Meanwhile, many GPUs sit idle in smaller data centers, mining operations and personal machines. Decentralized compute networks try to connect this idle supply with demand using a blockchain for coordination and payment.

sections.heading: The marketplace pattern
sections.body: Most compute networks share the same basic shape. A buyer describes a job and its requirements, such as GPU type, memory and duration. Providers offer their hardware, and some mechanism matches buyers to providers and sets a price. The blockchain records agreements and handles payment, often from funds held in escrow so providers know they will be paid. The interesting differences between networks lie in how matching, pricing and verification are done.

sections.heading: Akash: a reverse auction for cloud resources
sections.body: Akash is a general-purpose decentralized cloud built with the Cosmos SDK. A user, called a tenant, describes a deployment, including the containers to run and the resources needed. Providers then bid to host it, which is a reverse auction because sellers compete on price rather than buyers. The tenant chooses a bid, which creates a lease, and payments flow to the provider from an escrow account while the lease runs. Akash offers both CPUs and GPUs, so it can host ordinary web services as well as AI workloads.

sections.heading: Render: a GPU network with burn and mint
sections.body: Render began as a network for GPU rendering of 3D graphics and has expanded toward AI-related work. Creators submit jobs, and node operators with GPUs process them. Render uses a burn-and-mint model: users pay for work with tokens that are burned, and node operators are rewarded with newly minted tokens. The idea is to link changes in token supply to actual use of the network. Render moved its token from Ethereum to Solana, an example of how these networks can change their underlying chain.

sections.heading: What fits and what does not
sections.body: Not every AI task suits a marketplace of scattered machines. Training very large models requires thousands of GPUs exchanging data at very high speed, which works best inside a single data center with specialized networking. Inference, fine-tuning smaller models, batch jobs and rendering are much easier to split up, because each job can run on one machine or a small group. Data privacy is another constraint, since a provider can usually see the data and model it is running unless extra protections are used. Matching the workload to the network matters more than the marketing.

sections.heading: The verification problem
sections.body: When you rent compute from a stranger, you need some assurance that the job was actually run, and run correctly. A dishonest provider could return fake results, run a cheaper model, or quit midway. Networks use several tools to address this, including provider reputation, staked collateral that can be lost, redundant execution, and audits. Stronger guarantees come from verifiable computation methods such as cryptographic proofs or trusted hardware, which later modules cover. The less a network can verify, the more it relies on trust in providers.

concepts.definition: A processor built for many parallel calculations, used for most AI training and inference.
An auction where sellers compete by bidding down the price to win a buyer's job.
On Akash, the agreement formed when a tenant accepts a provider's bid, with payment drawn from escrow.
Funds locked under agreed rules and released to a party only when conditions are met.
A token design where payments for work are burned and service providers are rewarded with newly minted tokens.
Running the same job on several providers and comparing results to detect cheating or errors.

example.title: Deploying an inference server on Akash
example.body: A small team wants to host an open-source language model for their app. They write a deployment file describing the container image, the GPU model they need and the memory required, and submit it to Akash. Several providers bid, and the team accepts a bid that meets their requirements, creating a lease paid from escrow. If the provider performs badly, the team can close the lease and redeploy with a different provider.

modules.title: Data, provenance and decentralized storage
modules.summary: AI is only as good as its data, and models are just large files. Blockchains and decentralized storage can record where data and models came from, but they cannot certify that the data is true.
objectives: Explain content addressing and why it matters for datasets and model weights
Compare how IPFS, Filecoin and Arweave approach storage and persistence
Describe how hashes and timestamps create a provenance record
Explain what signed content credentials such as C2PA can and cannot show
Identify the limits of provenance, including licensing and data poisoning

sections.heading: Why data provenance matters for AI
sections.body: A model's behavior is shaped by the data it was trained on, so questions about that data matter. Was it licensed, was it collected with consent, and has it been tampered with? Model weights are also just files, and two files with the same name can contain very different models. Provenance means a verifiable record of where something came from and what happened to it. Without it, users have to trust a provider's word about which data and which model they are getting.

sections.heading: Content addressing
sections.body: A cryptographic hash turns any file into a short fingerprint, and changing even one bit of the file changes the fingerprint completely. Content addressing uses this fingerprint as the file's address, so you request data by what it is rather than by where it is stored. IPFS works this way, identifying content with a content identifier, or CID, derived from a hash. If you know the CID of a dataset or a set of model weights, you can check that a downloaded copy is exactly the right one. Content addressing proves integrity, but it does not by itself guarantee that anyone keeps storing the data.

sections.heading: Persistence: Filecoin and Arweave
sections.body: IPFS nodes only keep data they choose to keep, often called pinning, so files can disappear if nobody pins them. Filecoin adds a market where clients pay storage providers to keep data, and providers must submit cryptographic proofs. Proof-of-replication shows a provider stored a unique copy, and proof-of-spacetime shows it kept storing it over time, with collateral at risk if proofs fail. Arweave takes a different approach, asking for a one-time upfront payment that funds an endowment designed to pay for storage over the long term. The trade-off is roughly renewable contracts with ongoing proofs versus a single payment aimed at permanence.

sections.heading: Anchoring provenance on-chain
sections.body: A simple and powerful pattern is to publish a hash on a blockchain. If a team posts the hash of a training dataset or model weights in a transaction, anyone can later prove the file existed in that exact form by that block's time. A chain of such records can show which dataset version produced which model version. Signatures add identity, showing which key, and therefore which organization, published each record. The blockchain stores only small fingerprints, while the large files live in storage networks or ordinary servers.

sections.heading: Content credentials for media
sections.body: AI-generated images, audio and video make it harder to know where media came from. The C2PA standard, whose user-facing name is Content Credentials, attaches a signed manifest to a media file recording facts such as which tool created or edited it. A verifier can check the signature and confirm the file matches what the manifest describes. The specification itself says that this shows whether provenance data is intact and untampered, not whether the content is true. A file with no credentials is not proven fake, it simply lacks verifiable provenance.

sections.heading: What provenance cannot fix
sections.body: A hash on-chain proves that a file has not changed, not that the file is accurate, legal or fair. Garbage data anchored on a blockchain is still garbage, just provably unchanged garbage. Data poisoning, where an attacker slips misleading examples into training data, can be recorded perfectly by a provenance system without being detected. Licensing and consent are legal and social questions that a hash cannot answer. Provenance is best seen as a way to make claims checkable, so that responsibility can be traced, rather than a guarantee of quality.

concepts.definition: A verifiable record of where data or a model came from and how it was changed.
Locating data by a hash of its content rather than by the server or path where it is stored.
A content identifier in IPFS, derived from a hash of the content it names.
A Filecoin proof that a storage provider has kept storing specific data over a period of time.
A signed record attached to a media file describing its origin and edits, known to users as Content Credentials.
An attack that inserts misleading examples into training data to alter a model's behavior.

example.title: Publishing an open model with verifiable weights
example.body: A research group releases an open-weight model and stores the weight files on decentralized storage. They publish the hash of the weights and of the training data manifest in an on-chain transaction signed by their known address. A company that later downloads the model from a third-party mirror can hash the files and compare them to the on-chain record. A match proves they have the exact release, though it says nothing about whether the training data was properly licensed.

modules.title: Verifiable inference: zkML, optimistic and TEE approaches
modules.summary: Smart contracts cannot run large models themselves, so they need a way to trust a model's output. Zero-knowledge proofs, fraud proofs and trusted hardware each offer this with different costs and trust assumptions.
objectives: Explain why smart contracts cannot simply run AI models on-chain
Describe how zkML proves a model produced an output
Describe how optimistic verification uses fraud proofs and a challenge period
Describe how trusted execution environments provide attestations
Compare the trade-offs of each approach in cost, speed and trust
Explain why non-determinism complicates verification

sections.heading: The problem: trusting an output
sections.body: Blockchains execute every instruction on many nodes, which makes computation very expensive, far too expensive to run a modern AI model directly. So model inference happens off-chain, and a result is posted on-chain. The question is how a contract, or a user, can know the result really came from the claimed model running on the claimed input. Without verification, the party posting the result could submit anything. Verifiable inference is the family of techniques that try to close this gap.

sections.heading: zkML: proving the computation
sections.body: zkML applies zero-knowledge proofs to machine learning. The model's computation is expressed as a circuit, and the prover produces a succinct proof that running the committed model on a given input yields a specific output. A smart contract can verify this proof cheaply, without rerunning the model. The proof can also hide parts of the computation, such as private model weights or private inputs. The major drawback is cost: proving is far slower and more expensive than running the model normally, and the gap grows with model size, which makes zkML hardest to apply to large models.

sections.heading: Optimistic verification: assume, then challenge
sections.body: Optimistic approaches, sometimes called opML, borrow the design of optimistic rollups. A submitter posts a result and it is accepted by default, but there is a challenge period during which anyone can dispute it. In a dispute, the two parties narrow down their disagreement step by step until a single small computation step can be checked on-chain to decide who was wrong. Normal operation is cheap because nothing extra happens if no one cheats. The costs are latency, since results are only final after the challenge period, and the assumption that at least one honest party is watching and able to challenge.

sections.heading: TEEs: trusting hardware
sections.body: A trusted execution environment, or TEE, is an isolated area of a processor designed so that even the machine's operator cannot see or alter what runs inside. The hardware can produce a signed attestation stating which exact code is running, and the result can be signed by a key that never leaves the enclave. A verifier checks the attestation against the hardware vendor's certificates. This is fast and adds little overhead, so it can handle large models. The trade-off is trust in the hardware manufacturer, and past side-channel attacks on TEEs show that attestation is not an unconditional guarantee.

sections.heading: Comparing the trade-offs
sections.body: zkML offers the strongest guarantee because it relies on mathematics, but it is the most expensive and slowest to prove. Optimistic verification is cheap in the normal case but slow to finalize and dependent on active watchers with incentives to challenge. TEEs are fast and practical for large models but shift trust to a chip vendor and its security record. Some designs combine them, for example using TEEs for speed with an optimistic or zero-knowledge fallback. The right choice depends on how much value depends on the output and how quickly it must be final.

sections.heading: The determinism problem
sections.body: Verification usually assumes that the same model and input always give the same output. In practice, floating-point arithmetic on GPUs can produce tiny differences depending on hardware and the order of operations. Sampling settings such as temperature also add randomness unless the random seed is fixed. Optimistic disputes and redundant execution break if honest parties cannot agree on the exact output. Many verifiable inference designs therefore use deterministic arithmetic, such as fixed-point or quantized numbers, at some cost in speed or accuracy.

concepts.definition: Techniques that let others check that a specific model produced a specific output from a specific input.
Using zero-knowledge proofs to prove that a machine learning computation was performed correctly.
Accepting results by default and relying on fraud proofs during a challenge period to catch errors.
The window during which a posted result can be disputed before it becomes final.
An isolated processor area designed to protect code and data from the machine's operator.
A hardware-signed statement identifying the code running inside a trusted execution environment.

example.title: Choosing a method for an AI-driven contract
example.body: A lending protocol wants to use a small risk-scoring model to adjust collateral requirements. Because the model is small and the decision affects user funds, the team considers zkML, accepting slow proof generation in exchange for a mathematical guarantee. A different team running a large language model to summarize governance proposals chooses a TEE, since zkML would be impractical at that size and the output carries less direct financial risk. Both teams document what users must trust for each design.

modules.title: Risks: prompt injection, custody and hype
modules.summary: Connecting AI to money creates new attack surfaces and new ways to mislead. This module covers prompt injection, key custody, oracle-style trust in model outputs, and a framework for evaluating AI token claims.
objectives: Explain direct and indirect prompt injection against agents
Design agent controls that do not depend on the model behaving correctly
Identify common key custody mistakes in agent deployments
Explain why model outputs should be treated like untrusted oracle data
Apply a structured framework to evaluate AI-related token projects

sections.heading: Prompt injection
sections.body: Prompt injection is an attack where someone crafts text that causes a model to ignore its instructions and follow the attacker's instead. In direct injection, the attacker types the malicious instructions straight into the chat. Indirect prompt injection is more dangerous for agents: the attacker hides instructions in content the agent will read later, such as a web page, an email, a social media post or a token's metadata. Because a language model reads instructions and data as the same stream of tokens, it cannot reliably tell them apart. There is no known complete defense at the model level, so the defenses must be built around the model.

sections.heading: Defending agents that hold value
sections.body: The core rule is that model output is never authorization on its own. Any action that moves value should pass through checks the model cannot override, such as on-chain spending limits, allowlists and time-bound session keys. High-value or unusual actions should require human confirmation, and transactions can be simulated first to show their real effects. Separating roles also helps: an agent that reads untrusted content should not be the same component that holds signing authority. Assume an attacker will eventually get text in front of the model, and design so that the worst outcome is bounded.

sections.heading: Key custody
sections.body: Many agent incidents are plain key management failures. Private keys stored in environment variables, configuration files, code repositories or logs can leak through ordinary software bugs or careless sharing. A key should never be placed in the model's prompt or context, because the model may repeat it, and anything in the context can be extracted by injection. Safer setups keep keys in dedicated signing services, hardware security modules or multi-party computation wallets that enforce policy before signing. Agents should hold limited, revocable keys, while the owner's main keys stay out of reach.

sections.heading: Model outputs as oracle data
sections.body: When a smart contract acts on what a model says, the model is functioning like an oracle, an outside source of information the chain cannot check by itself. Every lesson from oracle design applies: single sources are fragile, inputs can be manipulated, and incentives to corrupt the source grow with the value at stake. A model can be steered by poisoned inputs, can hallucinate, and can be quietly swapped for a different model by whoever runs it. Defenses include verifiable inference, using several independent models or providers, sanity bounds on outputs, and delays that give humans time to react. The more value depends on an output, the more verification it needs.

sections.heading: Evaluating AI token claims
sections.body: AI is a popular label, so a structured framework helps separate substance from narrative. First, ask what the AI actually does and where it runs: many projects call a hosted API from an ordinary server, which is not on-chain AI. Second, ask whether the token has a necessary role, such as paying for a service, securing a network through staking, or governance, or whether it is attached for fundraising. Third, ask who controls the model, the keys and the upgrade rights, since an autonomous agent run by one team is still controlled by that team. Fourth, look for evidence you can check yourself, such as open code, on-chain usage paid by real users, and audits.

sections.heading: Red flags
sections.body: Some patterns should raise caution regardless of the technology. Claims of guaranteed returns from an AI trading system describe something no model can promise. Vague terms like decentralized AI with no explanation of what is decentralized, compute, data, training or governance, avoid scrutiny. An agent described as autonomous whose keys are held by an anonymous team is not autonomous in any meaningful sense. Usage numbers that only count token transfers, rather than paid use of the service, can describe speculation rather than demand.

concepts.definition: Crafted text that makes a model follow an attacker's instructions instead of its intended ones.
Prompt injection hidden in content an agent retrieves later, such as a web page or document.
A control that requires a person to approve certain actions before they are executed.
Running a transaction against current chain state without broadcasting it, to preview its effects.
A wallet whose signing key is split among several parties so no single machine holds the whole key.
The challenge of trusting outside information that a blockchain cannot verify by itself.

example.title: The Freysa challenge
example.body: In late 2024, a public game called Freysa put an AI agent in control of a prize pool, instructed never to approve an outgoing transfer, and charged players a rising fee to try to persuade it. A player won by convincing the agent that its approveTransfer function was meant for incoming payments, then offering a deposit, which led the agent to call the function and release the pool. No cryptography was broken, the agent was simply talked into misusing its own tool. The lesson is that a rule enforced only by a model's instructions is a suggestion, while a rule enforced by code is a boundary.

questions.prompt: What is a token in the context of a large language model?
options: A cryptocurrency used to pay for each AI query
A chunk of text the model processes as a number
A password that unlocks access to the model
A single complete sentence stored in the model's memory
questions.explanation: Text is split into tokens, such as word pieces or punctuation, and each is mapped to a number the model works with.

questions.prompt: What is the core task a large language model performs when generating text?
options: Looking up each answer in a verified fact database
Copying the closest matching document from training
Translating the prompt into a database query first
Predicting the next token from the tokens so far
questions.explanation: Generation is a loop of next-token prediction, which is why output is plausible text rather than looked-up fact.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between training and inference?
options: Training is cheap, while inference always needs huge data centers
Training happens per user; inference happens only once
Training adjusts the weights; inference uses them unchanged
Training reads prompts; inference reads the whole internet
questions.explanation: Training is the expensive phase that sets the weights, while inference runs the finished model to answer prompts without changing it.

questions.prompt: Why do language models sometimes hallucinate?
options: Their servers lose stored data whenever traffic gets too high
They deliberately insert errors to protect copyrights
They are optimized for plausible text, not verified truth
They only hallucinate when the prompt has a typo in it
questions.explanation: A model produces text that fits learned patterns, and it has no built-in check on whether a plausible answer is actually correct.

questions.prompt: A product claims its chatbot knows today's token prices. What is the best first question to ask?
options: How many languages can the chatbot speak?
Where does the live price data come from?
What color scheme does the chatbot use?
How long are the chatbot's typical replies?
questions.explanation: A model's own knowledge is fixed at its training cutoff, so current prices must be supplied by an external data source.

questions.prompt: What makes an AI agent different from a plain chatbot?
options: It can call tools and take actions in a loop
It always runs entirely inside a blockchain node
It never makes mistakes when it answers
It only works with images instead of text
questions.explanation: An agent places a model in a decide-act-observe loop with tools, so it can do things like send transactions, not just reply.

questions.prompt: Why is storing an agent's main private key on its own server risky?
options: Private keys stop working once they are copied to a server
Servers are not allowed to sign blockchain transactions
Compromising the server or the agent can drain everything
The key would be automatically shared with other agents
questions.explanation: With an unrestricted key, anyone who controls the server or manipulates the agent can move all the funds.

questions.prompt: What does a spending limit on an agent wallet do?
options: Lowers the gas price of each transaction it sends
Lets the agent borrow funds beyond its own balance
Hides the agent's balance from block explorers
Caps how much value the agent can move in a period
questions.explanation: A spending limit bounds the damage from a mistake or manipulation by capping value per transaction or per day.

questions.prompt: In account abstraction, what is a session key?
options: The seed phrase that recovers the owner's main wallet
A key that lets validators reorder pending transactions
A limited key a smart account accepts for set actions
A password used to log in to a centralized exchange
questions.explanation: A session key is valid only for certain contracts, amounts and time windows, so the owner's main key can stay offline.

questions.prompt: Why are limits enforced by a smart account contract stronger than limits in the agent's code?
options: They make every one of its transactions confirm faster on-chain
They let the agent skip paying transaction fees
They are written in a language models cannot read
They are checked on-chain even if the agent is compromised
questions.explanation: On-chain rules are enforced by the account contract, so a compromised or tricked agent cannot bypass them.

questions.prompt: On Akash, how is the price for a deployment determined?
options: Providers bid in a reverse auction and the tenant picks one
The network sets one fixed price for every GPU type
Validators vote on each new deployment's price in every block
The tenant pays whatever the first provider demands
questions.explanation: Akash uses a reverse auction where providers compete with bids, and accepting a bid creates a lease paid from escrow.

questions.prompt: In Render's burn-and-mint model, what happens to the tokens users pay for work?
options: They are sent directly to the founding team's treasury
They are locked forever as collateral for the GPUs
They are redistributed to all token holders equally
They are burned, and operators get newly minted tokens
questions.explanation: Payments are burned while node operators are rewarded from new issuance, linking supply changes to network usage.

questions.prompt: Which workload is hardest to run on a marketplace of scattered GPUs?
options: Training a very large model across thousands of GPUs
Running inference for a small open-source model
Rendering individual frames of a 3D animation
Running many independent batch jobs on separate machines
questions.explanation: Large-scale training needs very fast communication between GPUs, which works best inside one data center with specialized networking.

questions.prompt: Why do compute marketplaces often hold buyer payments in escrow?
options: So providers know funds exist and are paid as work runs
So the buyer can earn interest from the provider
So the network can safely skip verifying any of the work done
So payments become invisible on the blockchain
questions.explanation: Escrow locks the buyer's funds under agreed rules, assuring the provider of payment while the job or lease continues.

questions.prompt: What is the verification problem in decentralized compute?
options: Knowing a stranger's machine actually ran the job correctly
Proving that the buyer owns the tokens they spend
Checking that GPU prices match traditional clouds
Confirming that each provider's GPU hardware is entirely brand new
questions.explanation: A dishonest provider could return fake results or run a cheaper model, so networks need reputation, collateral, redundancy or proofs.

questions.prompt: What does content addressing let you verify about a downloaded set of model weights?
options: That the model was trained on properly licensed data
That the model's answers are factually accurate
That the file is exactly the one the hash identifies
That the storage provider will keep it permanently
questions.explanation: A content address is derived from a hash, so matching it proves integrity, but not licensing, accuracy or persistence.

questions.prompt: What does Filecoin's proof-of-spacetime demonstrate?
options: A provider owns the copyright for the data it stores
A provider has the fastest connection to the client
A provider has kept storing specific data over time
A provider has deleted the data once a deal ends
questions.explanation: Proof-of-spacetime shows ongoing storage of particular data, with provider collateral at risk if proofs fail.

questions.prompt: How does Arweave's storage model differ from Filecoin's?
options: Data is stored only on the uploader's own computer
One upfront payment funds an endowment for storage
Files are kept only until the next network upgrade
Storage is free but files are deleted after a year
questions.explanation: Arweave charges once and uses an endowment aimed at long-term storage, while Filecoin uses storage deals with ongoing proofs.

questions.prompt: According to the C2PA specification, what does a valid Content Credential show?
options: The media was captured by a real camera rather than generated by AI
The media contains no AI-generated elements anywhere
The media's creator has been verified by a government
Provenance data is intact and untampered, not that it is true
questions.explanation: C2PA validation checks the signature and that the file matches its manifest, and the spec states it makes no judgment on truth.

questions.prompt: A team anchors the hash of a poisoned training dataset on-chain. What does the record prove?
options: That this exact dataset existed unchanged by that time
That the dataset has been screened and cleared of any poisoning
That the data was collected with user consent
That models trained on it will be unbiased
questions.explanation: An on-chain hash proves existence and integrity of the exact file, so poisoned data is recorded faithfully rather than detected.

questions.prompt: Why do blockchains not run large AI models directly in smart contracts?
options: Smart contracts are not able to store any numbers
AI models are banned by most blockchain licenses
Models only run on phones, not on network nodes
Every node re-executes the work, making it far too costly
questions.explanation: On-chain computation is replicated across many nodes, so a modern model's workload would be prohibitively expensive.

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of zkML?
options: Its proofs are too large for any chain to verify
Generating proofs is very slow and costly for large models
It requires trusting the GPU manufacturer's attestation keys
It needs a week-long challenge window for disputes
questions.explanation: zkML gives cryptographic guarantees and cheap verification, but proving cost makes it practical mainly for small models.

questions.prompt: What security assumption does optimistic verification of inference rely on?
options: The hardware vendor's attestation keys stay secure
At least one honest party watches and can challenge
The model's weights are kept completely secret
Every node reruns the full model for each request
questions.explanation: Results are accepted by default, so safety depends on someone honest disputing a wrong result within the challenge period.

questions.prompt: What does a TEE attestation tell a verifier?
options: Which exact code is running inside the hardware enclave
That the model's output is factually correct
That the operator has staked enough collateral on-chain to cover losses
That a zero-knowledge proof was generated too
questions.explanation: An attestation is a hardware-signed statement of the enclave's code, so trust rests on the hardware vendor and its security.

questions.prompt: Why does GPU floating-point non-determinism matter for verifiable inference?
options: It makes models refuse to answer certain prompts
Honest parties may get slightly different outputs
It doubles the size of every zero-knowledge proof
It allows attackers to read the enclave's memory
questions.explanation: Disputes and redundant checks need everyone to agree on exact output, which is why many designs use deterministic fixed-point arithmetic.

questions.prompt: What makes indirect prompt injection especially dangerous for agents?
options: It only works when the user types in capital letters
Attackers hide instructions in content the agent reads
It requires physical access to the agent's server
It breaks the elliptic-curve signatures on the wallet
questions.explanation: Agents read web pages, posts and metadata, and a model cannot reliably separate instructions from data in that content.

questions.prompt: Which design best limits damage if an agent is successfully prompt-injected?
options: A stronger system prompt telling it never to obey attackers
A larger model that is better at spotting manipulation
On-chain limits and allowlists the model cannot override
A rule asking the model to double-check its own outputs
questions.explanation: Defenses that live in the model's instructions can be talked around, while code-enforced limits hold whatever the model is told.

questions.prompt: Why should a private key never be placed in an agent's prompt or context?
options: Keys in context make the model run more slowly
The model will refuse to start if it sees a key
Context windows automatically encrypt the key
Anything in context can be repeated or extracted
questions.explanation: A model may echo context contents, and an injection attack can coax it into revealing whatever its context holds.

questions.prompt: When a smart contract acts on a model's output, why is the model like an oracle?
options: It is an outside source the chain cannot verify itself
It produces random numbers that are provably fair
It is run by the same validators as the chain
It stores the chain's full transaction history
questions.explanation: Like any oracle, a model's output can be manipulated or wrong, so it needs redundancy, bounds or verifiable inference.

questions.prompt: A project calls its agent autonomous, but one anonymous team holds its keys and upgrade rights. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: The agent is fully decentralized because it uses AI
The agent is effectively controlled by that team
The agent is safe because it cannot be upgraded
The agent is trustless because its token is listed
questions.explanation: Whoever controls keys and upgrades controls the agent, so autonomy claims must be checked against who holds those powers.
